structured.name: Nauru
structured._source: wikidata (CC0); landBorders + naturalResources from CIA World Factbook (public domain)

prose.hook: Nauru is a single raised-coral island just south of the equator, and by most measures the smallest place of its kind on Earth: the third-smallest country overall, after the Holy See and Monaco, and the world's smallest island nation and smallest independent republic. It sits south of the Marshall Islands in the South Pacific, and like Banaba in Kiribati and Makatea in French Polynesia, it built its entire economic story around phosphate rock.
prose.physicalGeography: The island rises from a sandy beach through a fertile ring of land to a raised coral plateau at its center, where the phosphate deposits lie. Nauru has no land borders, being entirely surrounded by the South Pacific Ocean.
prose.climate: The climate is tropical with a monsoonal pattern, bringing a rainy season from November to February. The island is also subject to periodic droughts.
prose.economy: Nauru is classified as an upper-middle-income Pacific island country, though decades of phosphate mining have exhausted the resource and left the interior uninhabitable. The economy now relies on licensing fishing rights, hosting Australia's Regional Processing Centre, and foreign subsidies, having also served in the past as a tax haven. Its exports remain fish and phosphates, with industries spanning phosphate mining, offshore banking, and coconut products.
prose.peopleAndCulture: Ethnic Nauruans make up the large majority of the population, alongside smaller communities of I-Kiribati and Fijian descent. Nauruan, a distinct Pacific Island language, is the official tongue, though English is widely understood and used for most government and commercial purposes. Religiously, most Nauruans are Protestant, with a substantial Roman Catholic minority.
